one_liner: Pure-Swift arbitrary-precision integers (BInt) and fractions (BDouble), claimed about 2x faster than mini-gmp, not full GMP.
what_it_does: Provides BInt, a signed big integer stored as [UInt64] limbs plus a sign flag that conforms to SignedNumeric, BinaryInteger, Codable and Sendable, and BDouble, an exact big rational with a configurable decimal-printing precision. Operators mix freely with Int. Helpers cover factorial, gcd/lcm, permutations and combinations, modular exponentiation, radix conversion (bases 2-62), random BInts and pow/nthroot for BDouble. It is a dependency-free single source file (Swift-Big-Number-Core.swift) that can be dropped into a project or pulled in with SwiftPM or CocoaPods.
how_it_is_fast: Multiplication is Karatsuba above 48 limbs and schoolbook below, on 64-bit limbs using multipliedFullWidth. Decimal I/O works in base 10^18 chunks. Addition and multiplication skip zero limbs. The baseline, mini-gmp, is GMP's portable subset without assembly kernels, so the comparison measures portable code against portable code. A 2026-03 rewrite (PR #90) reported 70x on its own Fib 100000 benchmark, 6.5x on 270k-bit multiplication and 3.56x on factorial of 40,000 against the previous BInt, but division was unchanged (0.99x).
when_to_use: Swift apps on iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS or Linux that need big integers or exact rationals without linking GMP, for licensing or packaging reasons.
Moderate-size combinatorics, factorials, Fibonacci or exact-fraction arithmetic where multiplication and addition dominate.
Teaching or prototyping, where a single readable source file you can vendor beats a C dependency.
Generic Swift code over BinaryInteger that should also work with arbitrary-size integers.
when_not_to_use: Anything in C or C++: Swift only, with no C ABI. Use Boost.Multiprecision, mp++, FLINT or GMP instead.

Division-heavy or modular work (mod_exp, gcd on large values, modulo loops): multi-limb divMod is a bit-at-a-time shift-subtract loop with a full remainder shift per bit, so it is quadratic with a large constant. There is no Knuth Algorithm D, Barrett/Montgomery or subquadratic division.
Very large operands (millions of digits): no Toom-Cook or FFT multiplication beyond Karatsuba, and quadratic base-10^18 string conversion.
Cryptography: arithmetic is not constant-time and mod_exp is plain square-and-multiply over the slow division.

Workloads that need proven correctness: the tracker shows past wrong-result bugs (#78, Int(5) += BInt(10) gave 20; #80, a comparison returned the wrong answer for a variable Int vs a BInt, closed 2026-03-29), and #83 (BDouble nthroot(1024000, 2) loops forever) is still open.

integration.min_toolchain: Swift 5.5+ in practice, since BInt and BDouble declare Sendable; Package.swift and the podspec still say Swift 4.2 and the README says Xcode 9+/Swift 4+. Podspec targets iOS 11, macOS 10.11, watchOS 4, tvOS 11.
integration.platforms: Apple platforms and Linux; any CPU Swift targets (pure Swift, no assembly or SIMD)
integration.thread_safety: BInt and BDouble are value types declared Sendable, but BDouble.precision is a mutable global static that is not synchronised; not otherwise documented

gotchas: Benchmark numbers in the README (fib(100,000): 272 ms vs 530 ms for mini-gmp) predate the 2026-03 performance rewrite and give no hardware or build mode. The README says debug builds are more than 10x slower than release, so measure in release (-O).
In the README's performance paragraph 'GMP' means mini-gmp; full GMP was deliberately not compared and would likely win on large operands.

BDouble is an exact rational that auto-reduces by gcd, so long chains of operations grow numerators and denominators, and every gcd uses the slow division. pow and nthroot on BDouble are only accurate to the precision setting (docs say to compare with nearlyEqual).
Errors stop the program rather than being recoverable: division by zero, negative exponents and invalid bases trigger precondition or fatalError traps; String initialisers return nil on bad input.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only for Swift projects that cannot link GMP; every sibling in the catalog is C, C++ or Rust, and in C++ Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int or mp++ fill the same 'no external GMP' role with far better division and stronger evidence. Rust users have Malachite, ibig or dashu, which carry measured comparisons against real GMP.
verified_claims_summary: The only comparison is one first-party README sentence: BInt is about 2x faster than mini-gmp (GMP's portable C subset without assembly), adding via fib(100,000) in 272 ms vs 530 ms and multiplying more than twice as fast. No hardware, compiler, build mode, date or comparison harness is given; the repo's benchmarks time only BInt against its own saved baseline.
status_note: Maintained (v2.4.0 and a large performance rewrite merged 2026-03-29, 259 stars, MIT); one Swift file small enough to vendor, but irrelevant to C++ users and with a history of correctness bugs.
